source.title: Deep learning for deep learning performance: How much data is needed for segmentation in biomedical imaging?
source.authors: Junhyeok Lee; Hyungjin Chung; Minseok Suh; Jeong-Hoon Lee; Kyu Sung Choi

record.file_problem: The article text is intact. Figures are referenced but their plotted values are not available in the supplied text.
record.tranche_reason: The study sweeps training-data ratios and U-Net depth and reports test-set segmentation performance, but uses biomedical tasks and performance metrics rather than measuring double descent around an interpolation threshold.
record.gate_note: The study itself varies dataset size and model depth and reports test-set DSC trends. It does not measure training error or identify an interpolation threshold. Its references to double descent are citations, not results. LSTM forecasting errors are not rows because they measure the prediction model, not the claim’s scaling behavior.
record.test_reason: The study sweeps U-Net depth (3–6 layers) and training-data fraction and reports test DSC, but never measures training fit or locates an interpolation threshold. With only four widely spaced depths (6M–417M parameters on 700 images), it cannot show a peak near interpolation. Its results describe ordinary scaling and saturation. It cites Nakkiran et al. [10] only as motivation for possible degradation. Since its results cannot bear on whether any version holds, it does not test the claim.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that more data and greater depth improve segmentation up to diminishing returns (plateau ~80% data), and that an LSTM can forecast these performance curves to guide resource allocation.
record.recipe_differences: This is a biomedical segmentation study varying residual U-Net depth and training-data ratios, not an experiment designed to locate or measure double descent around an interpolation threshold.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported data and depth trends are evaluated separately on the Kvasir-SEG 2D polyp task and the BraTS 2020 3D whole-tumor task; the tested depth ranges differ.

fits_no_version.finding: In residual U-Nets on Kvasir-SEG and BraTS 2020, test DSC rises monotonically with data fraction and depth and plateaus beyond ~80% data. No interpolation regime is identified.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In medical segmentation with residual U-Nets, test performance saturates with data and depth rather than showing non-monotone scaling (regime relative to interpolation unknown).

record.problems: Only two datasets and a single architecture family are tested. The study does not measure training-set fit or locate an interpolation threshold. Numerical values for the scaling curves are not stated in the supplied text, and no uncertainty estimates are reported for those trends.
record.rows_left_out: The article describes IoU, Recall, and Precision trends and reports their best-configuration values, but the claim concerns test error and the text does not separately detail their scaling curves. Individual curve values are only referenced in figures and are not available in the supplied text. LSTM prediction MAEs in Tables 2–3 were omitted because they measure forecast accuracy rather than the claim’s scaling behavior.

record.verdict_notes: The reader labelled V1 'challenges'; this is removed. Absence of a peak across 4 depths with no training-fit or interpolation information is not evidence against model-wise double descent. Curve values exist only in figures, which are unavailable. The LSTM MAE tables were correctly excluded as rows.

versions.untested_parts: The study varies U-Net depth, but does not locate the training-set interpolation threshold or test whether a peak occurs near it.
Training epochs are not swept; the sequence used by the LSTM consists of dataset-size results, not epoch-wise task-model performance.
Data ratios are varied, but the study does not establish whether any ratio is near an interpolation threshold.
Only residual U-Nets are evaluated; there is no cross-model-class test of a general double-descent curve.
No single effective-complexity measure is tested as a predictor of peak location across size, epochs, and sample size.
The study does not manipulate label noise or regularization, or test multiple peaks or their disappearance.
The study does not re-express complexity using an effective parameter count or test whether that turns a second descent into a U-shaped curve.

rows.subject: residual U-Net (Kvasir-SEG)
rows.size_stated: 3, 4, 5, or 6 layers; parameter counts for depths 3–6 are 6.0, 25.6, 103.9, and 416.9 M
rows.operation_detail: Sweep model depth and measure test-set segmentation performance
rows.measure: Test-set DSC (higher indicates better segmentation performance)
rows.value: Performance improved with increasing model depth; gains were reported to plateau as complexity increased. The best configuration, 6 layers and 100% data, achieved DSC 0.86.
rows.note: The reported trend does not show a fall-rise-fall in error across the tested depths. The study does not establish where the training set first becomes exactly fitted.
rows.check: Monotone DSC gain with depth then plateau. No training-error or interpolation measure, and only 4 depths, so a model-wise peak could not be detected. Should not be read as absence of double descent.

rows.subject: residual U-Net (BraTS 2020)
rows.size_stated: 3 or 5 layers; parameter counts not stated
rows.operation_detail: Sweep model depth and measure test-set segmentation performance
rows.measure: Test-set DSC (higher indicates better segmentation performance)
rows.value: Performance improved with increasing model depth; the Discussion reports that improvement plateaued as complexity increased. The best configuration, 5 layers and 100% data, achieved DSC 0.79.
rows.note: Only depths 3 and 5 were compared. No fall-rise-fall trend is reported, and the interpolation threshold is not measured.
rows.check: Only two depths (3 and 5), with no parameter counts or training fit. Cannot show a fall-rise-fall curve.

rows.subject: residual U-Net (Kvasir-SEG)
rows.size_stated: 3, 4, 5, or 6 layers; parameter counts for depths 3–6 are 6.0, 25.6, 103.9, and 416.9 M
rows.operation_detail: Sweep training-data ratio and measure test-set segmentation performance

conditions.value: Kvasir-SEG; training n = 700; test set n = 200

rows.measure: Test-set DSC (higher indicates better segmentation performance)
rows.value: Metrics improved with larger training datasets, with gains plateauing beyond approximately 80% data usage.
rows.locator: Results, Task 1; Discussion; S2 and S6 Figs
rows.note: No increase in error is reported over the tested data ratios, but the study does not identify whether any condition is near the interpolation threshold named in V3.
rows.check: Data-ratio sweep shows improvement then plateau past ~80%. No interpolation threshold is identified, so there is no test of whether more data hurts near it. Small fluctuations at low ratios are attributed by the authors to training stochasticity.

rows.measure: Test-set DSC (higher indicates better segmentation performance)
rows.value: Performance improved with increasing training-data ratio and began to plateau significantly after the ratio exceeded 80%.
rows.note: The study does not identify an interpolation threshold, so this result cannot establish the behavior specifically near that threshold.
rows.check: Same as r3, for BraTS. No interpolation regime is identified.
